q.intro.text: Ana has the system three x plus two y equals sixteen, and five x minus four y equals twelve. She keeps the first equation and replaces the second by: the second, plus two times the first. That is eleven x equals forty-four. Does her new system have the same solution as the old one? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

q.cb.right.text: Back to Ana: you said the same solution. Right. Every step here replaced one equation and kept the other, and the crossing never moved.

q.cb.new.text: Back to Ana: you said a new solution. But every new line you drew went through the same crossing. Replacing one equation while keeping the other never moves it.

q.cb.keep.text: Back to Ana: you said only eleven x equals forty-four is left. But here x equals two alone was not the answer either: the kept equation gave y. The system keeps both equations.

q.cb.none.text: Every step replaced one equation and kept the other, and the crossing never moved.

e.intro.text: Four steps on Ana’s system. Press each step: the plane moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Graph both lines. They cross near four, two, but a graph only gives an estimate. To be exact we need algebra.

e.step1.text: Multiply the whole first equation by two: six x plus four y equals thirty-two. Every pair that fits three x plus two y equals sixteen fits this too: it is the same line, drawn dashed on top.

e.step2.text: Add it to the second: four y and minus four y cancel. Eleven x equals forty-four, so x equals four. That new equation is the upright line x equals four, and it goes through the same crossing.

e.step3.text: Back-substitute: three times four plus two y equals sixteen, so y equals two. The solution is the pair four, two. Check it in the equation we did not use: five times four minus four times two is twelve. It checks.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does the line x equals four pass through the same crossing?

e.why.ok.text: Four, two makes both equations true, so it makes their sum true too. Any equation built this way passes through the crossing.

e.why.icpt.text: The amber line meets the x-axis at sixteen thirds, not at four. The crossing is on x equals four because it fits both equations.

e.why.luck.text: It never misses: a pair that makes both equations true makes every sum of them true.

t.intro.text: Your turn: four x plus three y equals five, and three x minus two y equals eight. Done for you: eliminate y, because plus three y and minus two y already have opposite signs.

t.mult.text: Which multipliers turn three y and minus two y into opposites?

t.mult.ok.text: Yes: six y and minus six y. They cancel when you add.

t.mult.swap.text: Then the y-terms are nine y and minus four y: they do not cancel. Multiply each equation by the other one’s coefficient.

t.mult.one.text: Then the y-terms are six y and minus two y: they do not cancel. The second equation needs a multiplier too.

t.x.text: Add the new equations, eight x plus six y equals ten, and nine x minus six y equals twenty-four. What is x?

t.x.ok.text: Yes: seventeen x equals thirty-four, so x equals two.

t.x.stop.text: That is seventeen x. Divide by seventeen.

t.x.no.text: Add the left sides and the right sides: seventeen x equals thirty-four.

t.pair.text: Now find y and give the solution as a pair, x first, then y.

t.pair.ok.text: Yes: two, negative one. Check in the second: three times two, minus two times negative one, is eight. It checks.

t.pair.rev.text: Swapped: x comes first, and x is two.

t.pair.sign.text: Put x equals two into four x plus three y equals five: eight plus three y equals five, so three y equals negative three.

t.pair.no.text: Put x equals two into one of the equations and solve for y.

p.intro.text: Sam solves two x minus three y equals six, and negative four x plus six y equals negative twelve. He adds two times the first to the second, gets zero equals zero, and writes: so x is zero and y is zero, the solution is zero, zero. Is Sam right?

p.build.text: Sam is wrong. Build the proof: pick the reason behind each claim.

p.test.text: Test it first: put zero, zero into the first equation. Then build the proof: pick the reason behind each claim.

p.c1.text: Right: zero is not six, so zero, zero is not even on the amber line.

p.c2.text: Right: the teal line lies exactly on the amber one. Two equations, one line.

p.c3.text: Right: three, zero and six, two work, one, one does not. Infinitely many solutions, all on one line.

p.no.zero.text: The letters cancelling does not make them zero: zero equals zero says nothing about x or y.

p.no.every.text: Zero equals zero is always true, but the first equation still has to hold: one, one gives two minus three, negative one, not six.

p.no.many.text: Two different lines cross at most once. These are the same line.

p.no.other.text: That reason belongs to another claim. Read the claim with the empty gap.

p.done.text: Proved: every point of the line two x minus three y equals six is a solution, and nothing else. Sam’s zero, zero is not one of them.
